name: Quantitative evaluation, version 2
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: SIG's Quantitative Evaluation. Seventeen questions in 60 minutes with a calculator, rising from quick expected values to multi-stage Bayes and ruin.
description: This is the reported format of SIG's Quantitative Evaluation, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. You have 17 questions in 60 minutes. A calculator is allowed, but the app has none, so have a basic one ready. The questions start with quick expected values and end with multi-stage Bayes and gambler's ruin. Some take a choice, others a number to three decimal places. A wrong answer scores 0, and you may change answers until you submit. Other reports give 16 questions in 20 minutes; this mock follows the longer one. This is version 2 of 3.

items.title: Same colour pays
items.question: You draw two cards from a well-shuffled 52-card deck, without replacement. You are paid £51 if they are the same colour. What is a fair price to play once?

options.why: You drew with replacement. After the first card, only 25 of the other 51 share its colour.
You counted two reds only. Two blacks pay as well.
You left the first card in the deck. Only 25 cards of its colour remain.

feedback.correct: The second card matches the first with chance $\tfrac{25}{51}$, so the price is £25.00.
feedback.generic: Fix the first card. Then ask how many of the other 51 cards share its colour.

explain.text: Whatever the first card, 25 of the other 51 share its colour. So the fair price is $51 \times \tfrac{25}{51} = 25$ pounds. Check: two reds or two blacks, $2 \times \tfrac{26 \times 25}{52 \times 51} = \tfrac{25}{51}$.

items.title: Record days
items.question: Five days' closing prices, all different, are shown in a random order. A day is a record if its price beats every earlier day's, and day 1 always counts. What is the expected number of records?

options.why: You gave every day a half. Day $k$ is a record only when it is the highest of the first $k$ days, chance $\tfrac1k$.
You counted only day 1. Later days can still beat every day before them.
You left out day 1, which is always a record.

feedback.correct: Day $k$ is a record with chance $\tfrac1k$, so the count averages $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac15 \approx 2.28$.
feedback.generic: Give each day an indicator. Day $k$ is a record when it is the highest of the first $k$ days.

explain.text: Day $k$ is a record when it is the highest of the first $k$ days, chance $\tfrac1k$. By linearity the expected count is $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac15 = \tfrac{137}{60} \approx 2.28$. Check: the 120 orders hold 274 records in all, and $\tfrac{274}{120} = \tfrac{137}{60}$.

items.title: A six rolls on
items.question: You pay £1 to roll a fair die. Each six pays £4 and earns a free roll. Any other face ends the game. What is your expected profit per game?

options.why: You stopped after the first roll. Each six brings another chance at £4.
You assumed one six per game. On average a game holds only $\tfrac15$ of a six.
You counted only the fee. Sixes pay some of it back.

feedback.correct: A game holds $\tfrac15$ of a six on average, worth £0.80, so the profit is −£0.20.
feedback.generic: Let $G$ be the expected payout of one roll, free rolls included. A six pays £4 and then $G$ again.

explain.text: The expected payout satisfies $G = \tfrac16(4 + G)$, so $G = \tfrac45$ and the profit is $0.80 - 1 = -0.20$ pounds. Check: a game holds $k$ sixes with chance $(\tfrac16)^k \tfrac56$, which averages $\tfrac{1/6}{5/6} = \tfrac15$ of a six.

items.title: Calling the ranks
items.question: You turn the 52 cards of a shuffled deck one at a time. As you turn, you call ace, two, three and so on up to king, then start again at ace. What is the expected number of cards that match the rank you call?

options.why: You treated it as a shuffle with one match on average. There are 52 calls, each right with chance $\tfrac{1}{13}$.
You expected one match per rank. Each call is right only one time in 13.
That is one card’s chance, $\tfrac{1}{13}$. Add it over all 52 cards.

feedback.correct: Each card matches its call with chance $\tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac{1}{13}$, and $52 \times \tfrac{1}{13} = 4$.
feedback.generic: Give each of the 52 places an indicator for a match, and add their chances.

explain.text: Any place is equally likely to hold any of the 52 cards, and 4 of them have the called rank. So each place matches with chance $\tfrac{1}{13}$, and linearity gives $52 \times \tfrac{1}{13} = 4$. The matches are not independent, but linearity does not need them to be.

items.title: Three rising faces
items.question: You roll a fair six-sided die three times. What is the chance that each roll is strictly higher than the one before? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: Choose the 3 faces, $\binom63 = 20$ ways, and they rise in one order only: $\tfrac{20}{216} \approx 0.093$.
feedback.generic: Count the rising rolls. Each set of three different faces gives exactly one.

byKey.ties: You ignored ties. Only rolls with three different faces can rise.
byKey.either: That counts rising or falling rolls. Only the rising order counts.
byKey.different: That is the chance all three faces differ. Only one of their six orders rises.

explain.text: A rising roll is fixed by its set of three faces, so $\binom63 = 20$ of the 216 rolls rise. That gives $\tfrac{20}{216} = \tfrac{5}{54} \approx 0.093$. Check: all three differ with chance $\tfrac{120}{216}$, and one of the six orders rises, $\tfrac{120}{216} \times \tfrac16 = \tfrac{20}{216}$.

items.title: Where the aces sit
items.question: Five cards are dealt from a well-shuffled 52-card deck. You are told exactly two of the five are aces. What is the chance the first card dealt is an ace?

options.why: You ignored the news. With two aces among five cards, each place holds one with chance $\tfrac25$.
You allowed for one ace only. Two of the five places hold aces.
You treated ace or not as even. Three of the five places hold other cards.

feedback.correct: The two aces are equally likely to sit in any 2 of the 5 places, so the chance is $\tfrac25$.
feedback.generic: Given the count, every placing of the two aces among the five places is equally likely.

explain.text: Each of the $\binom52 = 10$ placings of the two aces is equally likely. The first place is among them in $\binom41 = 4$ placings, so the chance is $\tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac25$. Check: the five places hold 2 aces in all, and by symmetry each holds $\tfrac25$ of one.

items.title: Matching head counts
items.question: You and a colleague each toss a fair coin 3 times. What is the chance you get the same number of heads?

options.why: You treated 0, 1, 2 and 3 heads as equally likely. One or two heads are three times as likely as none.
That is the chance your two sequences match exactly. Different orders with the same count also match.
You counted one or two heads only. Both getting none, or both getting three, also match.

feedback.generic: Find the chance of each head count. Then add the chance that both of you land on it.

explain.text: Each count $k$ has chance $\tfrac{1}{8}\binom3k$, so a match has chance $\tfrac{1 + 9 + 9 + 1}{64} = \tfrac{5}{16}$. Check: a match means your heads plus your colleague’s tails make exactly 3 of 6 tosses, chance $\tfrac{1}{64}\binom63 = \tfrac{20}{64}$.

items.title: Higher or lower
items.question: I pick a whole number from 1 to 1,000. After each guess I say higher, lower or correct. What is the fewest guesses that always find my number, counting the correct one?

options.why: You rounded $\log_2 1000 \approx 9.97$ down. Nine guesses can settle only 511 numbers.
You counted three answers per guess, as on a balance. "Correct" settles only the number guessed.
You assumed each guess rules out two numbers. Guessing the middle rules out half of them.

feedback.correct: $k$ guesses settle at most $2^k - 1$ numbers, and $2^{10} - 1 = 1023$ is the first to reach 1,000.
feedback.generic: Count how many numbers $k$ guesses can settle in the worst case.

explain.text: A first guess settles 1 number and splits the rest into two sides, so $k$ guesses settle at most $N_k = 1 + 2N_{k-1} = 2^k - 1$. Nine guesses cover only 511 and ten cover 1,023, so 10 always suffice and 9 do not. Guessing the middle of the range each time reaches the bound.

items.title: A survey with a coin
items.question: A survey asks traders a sensitive yes-or-no question. Each secretly tosses a fair coin: on heads they answer truthfully, and on tails they say yes. In all, 60% say yes. What is the chance that a trader who said yes is truly a yes? Give three decimal places.

widget.label: Chance a yes is a true yes

feedback.correct: The true share $p$ solves $\tfrac12 p + \tfrac12 = 0.6$, so $p = 0.2$, and $\tfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \tfrac13$.
feedback.generic: First find the true share of yeses, $p$, from $0.6 = \tfrac12 p + \tfrac12$.

byKey.share: That is the true share of yeses. Now condition on hearing a yes.
byKey.said: That is the share who said yes, not the chance a yes is true.
byKey.heads: You counted only the yeses given on heads. A true yes who tosses tails also says yes.

explain.text: A yes comes from heads with a true yes, $\tfrac12 p$, or from tails, $\tfrac12$, so $p = 0.2$. Every true yes says yes, whatever the coin, so $P(\text{true} \mid \text{yes}) = \tfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \tfrac13 \approx 0.333$. Check: of 1,000 traders, 200 are true yeses and 600 say yes.

items.title: A total divisible by 7
items.question: You roll a fair die again and again, keeping a running total. What is the expected number of rolls until the total is first a multiple of 7?

options.why: You left out the first roll. From a total of 0, one roll can never reach a multiple of 7.
You divided 7 by the average roll, 3.5. The total often jumps past 7 and must wait for a later multiple.
You used $\tfrac{1}{2/7}$, as if each roll landed on a multiple with the long-run chance $\tfrac27$. That chance is per total, not per roll.

feedback.correct: After the first roll, exactly one face of six turns the total into a multiple of 7, so the wait is $1 + 6 = 7$.
feedback.generic: Track the remainder of the total on division by 7. From a non-zero remainder, how many faces bring it to 0?

explain.text: The first roll leaves a remainder from 1 to 6, never 0. From any non-zero remainder exactly one face brings it to 0, so each later roll succeeds with chance $\tfrac16$. The wait is $1 + 6 = 7$ rolls.

items.title: Paying to look again
items.question: Each draw costs £2 and shows an amount uniform between £0 and £100. You may stop after any draw and take the last amount shown. Under the best rule, what is the game worth, net of every draw’s cost?

options.why: You took the first draw: £50 on average, less its £2.
You set the gain from one more draw to $\tfrac{(100 - t)^2}{100}$. Its average is half that.
You took the average draw and forgot what each draw costs.

feedback.correct: Keep the first amount above $t$, where one more draw gains $\tfrac{(100 - t)^2}{200} = 2$. So $t = 80$, and the game is worth £80.
feedback.generic: Let $V$ be the game’s value. You should keep an amount exactly when it beats $V$.

explain.text: With value $V$, a draw is worth $E[\max(U, V)] - 2 = V + \tfrac{(100 - V)^2}{200} - 2$, and this must equal $V$. So $(100 - V)^2 = 400$ and $V = 80$. Check: stopping above 80 takes 5 draws on average, costing £10, and a kept amount averages £90.

items.title: A six before any five
items.question: You roll a fair die until the first six. You are told no five came up before it. Given that, what is the expected number of rolls, the six included? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: The wait for the first 5 or 6 averages 3 rolls. The news only says which of the two ended it.
feedback.generic: Look at the first roll that shows a 5 or a 6. How long is that wait, and does the news change it?

byKey.plain: That ignores the news. Games with no five before the six tend to be short.
byKey.five-faces: You rolled a five-faced die instead. The news also favours games that end quickly.

explain.text: The first 5 or 6 comes after a geometric wait with chance $\tfrac13$, so 3 rolls on average. That face is a 5 or a 6 with even chances, independent of the wait, so the answer stays 3. Check: $\sum_n n (\tfrac46)^{n-1} \tfrac16 = \tfrac32$, divided by $P(\text{no five first}) = \tfrac12$, gives 3.

items.title: The ball that moved
items.question: Urn A holds 3 red and 2 blue balls; urn B holds 2 red and 2 blue. One ball is moved at random from A to B, unseen. Then a ball drawn at random from B is red. What is the chance the moved ball was red?

options.why: That is the chance before the draw. A red draw from B makes a red move more likely.
That is the chance of a red move and a red draw together. Divide by the chance of a red draw.
That is the chance of drawing red from B. You need the moved ball’s colour given that draw.

feedback.generic: Split on the moved ball’s colour. B then holds 5 balls, 3 of them red or 2 of them red.

explain.text: A red move leaves B with 3 red of 5, and a blue move with 2 red of 5. So $P(\text{red moved} \mid \text{red drawn}) = \tfrac{9/25}{9/25 + 4/25} = \tfrac{9}{13}$. Check: of 25 equally likely pairs of moved and drawn ball, 13 draws are red, 9 of them after a red move.

items.title: An order passed twice
items.question: A client's order is a buy with chance 0.3 and otherwise a sell. It is relayed through two desks, and each swaps buy and sell by mistake with chance $\tfrac14$, independently. The trader receives a buy. What is the chance the client meant buy? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: The order arrives right with chance $\tfrac58$, so $\tfrac{0.3 \times 5/8}{0.3 \times 5/8 + 0.7 \times 3/8} = \tfrac{5}{12} \approx 0.417$.
feedback.generic: First find the chance the order comes through right after two desks: no swap, or two swaps.

byKey.one-desk: That allows for one desk only. Two swaps cancel, so the order arrives right with chance $\tfrac58$.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the order arrived.
byKey.intact: That is the chance the order arrives unchanged. Now weigh it against the prior.

explain.text: Through two desks the order arrives right with chance $(\tfrac34)^2 + (\tfrac14)^2 = \tfrac58$. Bayes gives $\tfrac{0.3 \times 5}{0.3 \times 5 + 0.7 \times 3} = \tfrac{1.5}{3.6} = \tfrac{5}{12} \approx 0.417$. Check: of 160 orders, 48 buys give 30 received buys and 112 sells give 42, so $\tfrac{30}{72} = \tfrac{5}{12}$.

items.title: Splitting an unfinished match
items.question: Two equally good players play games for a £64 pot, and the first to win 4 games takes it. They must stop with Ann ahead by 2 games to 1. What is her fair share of the pot?

options.why: You split the pot evenly. Ann’s lead is worth something.
You split by games won, 2 to 1. The share should follow her chance of winning.
You split by games still needed, 3 to 2 her way. The share should follow her chance of winning.

feedback.correct: Ann needs 2 wins before Bob gets 3. In 4 more games she needs at least 2, chance $\tfrac{11}{16}$, so £44.
feedback.generic: Ann needs 2 more wins and Bob needs 3. Imagine 4 more games are always played.

explain.text: Play 4 more games: Ann wins exactly when she takes at least 2 of them, $1 - \tfrac{1 + 4}{16} = \tfrac{11}{16}$. Her share is $\tfrac{11}{16} \times 64 = 44$ pounds. Check: from 2 needed against 3, first-step analysis gives the same $\tfrac{11}{16}$.

items.title: Up two, down one
items.question: Each bet wins £2 with chance $\tfrac13$ and loses £1 with chance $\tfrac23$. You start with £1 and stop when you have £0, or £4 or more. What is the chance you finish with £4 or more? Give three decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of finishing with £4 or more

feedback.generic: Let $P_k$ be the chance of finishing with £4 or more from £$k$. Condition on the next bet.

byKey.fair: The bet is fair, but $\tfrac14$ assumes you stop exactly on £4. A win from £3 lands on £5, so the chance is lower.
byKey.two-wins: That counts two straight wins only. You can fall back and try again.
byKey.no-return: You dropped the paths that fall back to £1. Solve the first-step equations instead.

explain.text: From £1 a win goes to £3 and a loss ends it, so $P_1 = \tfrac13 P_3$, with $P_3 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 P_2$ and $P_2 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 P_1$. Substituting gives $\tfrac{23}{27} P_1 = \tfrac{5}{27}$, so $P_1 = \tfrac{5}{23} \approx 0.217$. Check: ending on £4 with chance $\tfrac{2}{23}$ and on £5 with $\tfrac{3}{23}$ averages $\tfrac{8 + 15}{23} = 1$ pound, as a fair game must.

items.title: Avoiding the favourite
items.question: Four players enter a knockout: you, the favourite and two others. The semi-final pairs are drawn at random. You beat the favourite with chance 0.3 and each other player with chance 0.6. The favourite beats each other player with chance 0.8. What is your chance of winning the event? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Split on the draw: you meet the favourite in the semi-final with chance $\tfrac13$.

byKey.always-fav: That assumes you meet the favourite for sure. The draw keeps you apart two times in three.
byKey.never-fav: That assumes you never face the favourite. She often reaches the final.

explain.text: With chance $\tfrac13$ you meet the favourite first and win with $0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18$. Otherwise you win your semi-final with 0.6 and then face her with 0.8, so you win with $0.6 \times (0.8 \times 0.3 + 0.2 \times 0.6) = 0.216$. Altogether $\tfrac13 \times 0.18 + \tfrac23 \times 0.216 = 0.204$.
